title: Evaluating online sources
examples: How do I know if a website is telling the truth?
What should I check when I find information online?
Is it okay to trust everything I read on social media?

explain.say: When you find information online, you must check who wrote it.
Next, always look at the date to see how current the information is.
Also, try to figure out the main reason the source was created.
A powerful skill is lateral reading when you check other sites.
For example, if a site claims a new scientific discovery, check major university sites.
In real life, when you read about a local event, check the official council website.

items: Look for the official domain name.
See if other local news sites mention it.

draw.text: Real life: Check official council site.

faq.q: How many sources should I check for one fact?
faq.a: It is best to check at least three different, reputable sources. You can also ask if the source is peer-reviewed.
asks: Do I need to check everywhere?

faq.q: What is the difference between bias and opinion?
faq.a: Bias is when someone unfairly favours one side, while opinion is just a personal belief. Look for strong emotional language in biased texts.
asks: Is bias the same as having an opinion?

faq.q: If a website looks professional, can I trust it?
faq.a: No, a professional look can be faked by anyone. You must still check the author and the date carefully.
asks: Does good design mean it is true?
Can I trust a fancy website?

faq.a: It means leaving the source you are on to check what reliable outside sources say about it. You are reading across the web.
asks: What is reading across the web?
Should I just read the article deeply?

faq.a: Wikipedia is a good starting point, but you must use its references to find primary sources. Always check the original source cited.
asks: Can I use Wikipedia for my project?

facts: Reputable sources often include academic institutions or established news agencies.
Checking the date helps you know if information is outdated or current.
Lateral reading involves opening new tabs to verify claims.
Be wary of sources whose main purpose seems only to sell something.

quiz.say: A website about climate change cites studies from NASA and the World Meteorological Organization. Which element should you trust most?

options.show: The use of strong, urgent language.
options.say: The use of strong, urgent language.

options.show: The fact that it is published online.
options.say: The fact that it is published online.

options.show: The citations to major scientific bodies.
options.say: The citations to major scientific bodies.

quiz.why: Citing established scientific bodies shows the information is backed by expert research.

wrong.0: Strong language is often used to persuade, not necessarily to prove facts.
wrong.1: Being online does not automatically make information true or reliable.
wrong.3: A nice design can be used by anyone, regardless of the facts.

quiz.say: You read a blog post with no author listed. What is the first thing you should do?

options.show: Search for the topic on a recognized encyclopedia site.
options.say: Search for the topic on a recognized encyclopedia site.

options.show: Just change the headline to sound more official.
options.say: Just change the headline to sound more official.

options.show: Ask a friend who also read it.
options.say: Ask a friend who also read it.

quiz.why: When the author is unknown, you must find the information through a known, reliable source.

wrong.1: Assuming trust without checking is the biggest mistake in research.
wrong.2: Changing words does not change the underlying lack of evidence.
wrong.3: Friends can share misinformation without meaning to mislead you.

quiz.say: A source's purpose is to convince you that Brand X phone is the best. What is this source doing?

options.show: It has a commercial purpose and may be biased.
options.say: It has a commercial purpose and may be biased.

quiz.why: When the goal is to sell something, the information is usually biased towards that sale.

wrong.0: A neutral summary would present pros and cons without favouring one.
wrong.2: Selling something is a specific type of purpose, not just general information.
wrong.3: Objective reports try to remain neutral, which selling products rarely does.
